findings.title: Exhausted federated recovery credential is deleted with local-only API
findings.body: The lookup was changed to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which can return a federated credential. The subsequent call to authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById() only removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store. If the found recovery credential came from an external user storage provider, this deletion will not affect that credential (and may target an ID that is not local). As a result, an exhausted federated recovery-code credential can remain present while Keycloak only adds the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, leaving inconsistent credential state and potentially stale credentials visible.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() can break login page rendering
findings.body: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) returns an Optional, but the bean immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get(). It also calls recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() on line 21. If the recovery credential is missing (for example, removed concurrently, not returned by external storage, or no remaining codes exist), this throws NoSuchElementException and can surface as a 500 error while rendering the login page instead of failing gracefully or redirecting to the required action.

findings.title: Existing local recovery-code credential is not cleaned up when user storage creation succeeds
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() treats a true result from user.credentialManager().updateCredential() as success in user storage and does not remove any pre-existing local recovery-authn-code credential. If a user previously had locally stored recovery codes and their user storage later accepts recovery codes, both the old local credential and the new federated credential can coexist. This leaves stale backup codes behind and makes the effective credential set ambiguous; recovery credentials should be replaced or explicitly cleaned up.

findings.title: Plaintext recovery codes are handed to external user storage
findings.body: The helper serializes the generated raw recovery codes and passes them to user storage via UserCredentialModel. Keycloak's local path stores hashed recovery codes, but this code sends the full plaintext list to any external user storage provider. The included test storage also persists these values unhashed. Because recovery codes are bearer secrets, this can lead to plaintext persistence or exposure in external systems. If external storage can operate on hashed values, those should be used; otherwise the security contract should be explicit.

findings.title: Test storage and test do not enforce one-time use of recovery codes
findings.body: The test storage's isValid() for recovery codes only checks whether the submitted code exists in the stored list; it never removes or marks the code as used. The added test logs in once with a recovery code but does not verify that the same code is rejected on a second use. Since recovery codes are one-time credentials, this leaves the new user-storage path untested for replay and the sample storage implementation demonstrates replayable recovery codes.

findings.title: getCredentials() can throw NullPointerException for missing user
findings.body: getCredentials() calls getMyUser(user) and then immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes. getMyUser() can return null if the user is not present in the map, while other methods in this class guard against a missing user. If getCredentials() is invoked for an unknown user, the provider throws NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.
